stops.name: Arras, the prisoner and the portrait
stops.campa: Sold for ten thousand livres tournois, a king's ransom paid by England through the taxes of conquered Normandy, she passes into the Duke of Burgundy's city of Arras on the long road to Rouen. Here a Scot shows her a painting of herself: full-armed, kneeling on one knee, presenting a letter to her king. It is the only image of herself she ever speaks of seeing, and she speaks of it to her judges without vanity, a girl looking at the legend already detaching itself from her. The University of Paris has claimed her for the Inquisition; the Church militant has become the hunting arm of England.
stops.quote: I saw at Arras a painting in the hands of a Scot: it showed me all armed, presenting a letter to my king, kneeling on one knee.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, session of 3 March 1431

stops.name: Le Crotoy, the sea-castle on the Somme
stops.campa: In the English sea-fortress of Le Crotoy, where the Somme meets the Channel, the Maid of the rivers first sees the tide. A captive chancellor of Amiens says mass in the castle daily and hears her in confession; he goes out saying he has never seen a better Christian. The good wives of Abbeville take boat down the estuary to visit and comfort her, and she thanks them and commends herself to their prayers. Then at low water she is ferried across the bay to Saint-Valery, the crossing where the Conqueror once waited for his wind, and the road runs now only one way: Eu, Dieppe, Rouen.

stops.name: Rouen, the tower of the castle of Bouvreuil
stops.campa: Two days before Christmas she is brought into Rouen, capital of English France, and lodged not in a Church prison with women to attend her, as law requires of an ecclesiastical accused, but in the castle of Bouvreuil, in a tower cell, irons on her feet, chained by night to a beam, watched day and night by English guards of the meanest sort. An iron cage is forged to hold her upright, the canon remembers, though the chains suffice. The child-king Henry VI keeps court in the same castle. Cauchon, bishop of ruined Beauvais, assembles his assessors and buys his jurisdiction. The instrument of the Passion is prepared.

stops.name: Rouen, the first public session in the royal chapel
stops.campa: Before Cauchon and some forty doctors in the chapel royal of Rouen castle, the girl of nineteen is brought in her page's suit, chained, alone against the University of Paris. Required to swear on the Gospels to answer everything, she makes at once the distinction that holds through fifteen interrogations: of her father and mother and her deeds since she took the road to France, gladly; of her revelations from God, to no man here, though they cut off her head. She takes the oath kneeling, hands on the missal, on her own terms. Asked to say the Paternoster: hear me in confession and I will say it gladly.
stops.quote: Of my father and my mother, and of what I have done since I took the road to France, I will gladly swear; but the revelations that have come to me from God I have never told or revealed to anyone save to Charles my king; nor will I reveal them though my head be cut off.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, session of 21 February 1431

stops.name: Rouen, the answer on the grace of God
stops.campa: In the robing chamber at the end of the great hall, before sixty judges, the theologian Beaupère lays the perfect trap: does she know herself to be in God's grace? Yes condemns her of presumption, no out of her own mouth. The notaries record that the questioners themselves were stupefied by her answer, and the court adjourns soon after. The same day she tells them how the voice woke her at noon; the voice is beautiful, sweet and low, and speaks the tongue of France. Asked another day if Saint Margaret speaks English: why should she, who is not on the English side?
stops.quote: If I am not in the grace of God, may God put me there; and if I am, may God so keep me. I should be the saddest creature in the world if I knew I were not in the grace of God.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, session of 24 February 1431

stops.name: Rouen, the prison sessions and the promise of Paradise
stops.campa: The public sessions done, Cauchon carries the interrogation into her cell, small parties of examiners at the bedside of a chained girl. Here the record reaches its highest places: her saints have promised to lead her to Paradise, as she asked of them; she is as sure of it as if she were there already. The judges seize on it: if sure of salvation, why confess? She answers that one cannot be too careful. Asked about her leap, the sign given the king, her banner, she answers or refuses with the same unhurried courtesy. The judges call it the great promise; she calls it a treasure.
stops.quote: Take everything peacefully; do not fret at your martyrdom; you shall come at last into the kingdom of Paradise... I hold to it as firmly as if I were there already.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, prison session of 14 March 1431

stops.name: Rouen, the torture chamber of the great tower
stops.campa: They bring her into the great tower where the instruments are laid out and the executioners stand ready, and threaten her with the question. She looks at the rack and gives them the answer that closes the argument of force forever: tear her limb from limb and drive the soul from her body, she will say nothing else; and whatever they wring from her she will afterward declare was wrung by force and worth nothing. The judges withdraw and vote: torture would profit nothing, and would soil a beautiful trial, un si beau procès, with the mark of the tongs. Three days later they decide to forgo it.
stops.quote: Truly, if you were to tear me limb from limb and drive my soul out of my body, I would tell you nothing more; and if I did say anything to you, afterward I should always declare that you had made me say it by force.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, session of 9 May 1431

stops.name: The cemetery of Saint-Ouen, the abjuration
stops.campa: On two scaffolds in the abbey cemetery, before cardinals, bishops, a great crowd, the preacher Érard cries that Charles her king is a heretic; led to the edge of the fire, she interrupts him to defend the king with her life. Then the sentence is begun, the executioner's cart waits, in the noise and pressing, promised her life, the Church's prison, women about her, she yields and repeats a short abjuration, signing with a cross while something like a laugh passes over her face. They read her instead into perpetual prison on the bread of sorrow and the water of affliction, and return her to the English chains.
stops.quote: I dare say and swear, on pain of my life, that he is the most noble Christian of all Christians, and best loves the faith and the Church of all.
stops.quote_source: Rehabilitation testimony of Jean Massieu and others on the sermon of Guillaume Érard, 24 May 1431

stops.name: Rouen, the relapse in the cell
stops.campa: Four days in a woman's dress among English guards who mock and mishandle her, the promises broken: no Church prison, no women, the chains still on. On Trinity Sunday her man's clothes are found on her again; whether left in the sack by design or resumed in defence of her body, the trap shuts either way. When the judges come on Monday she is wholly herself again: her voices have told her the great pity of the treason she consented to when she abjured to save her life. Cauchon comes out to the waiting Englishmen, the witnesses say, laughing: farewell, be of good cheer; it is done.
stops.quote: What I said, I said for fear of the fire... God has told me by Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret of the great pity of the treason to which I consented in abjuring to save my life: I damned myself to save my life.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, session of 28 May 1431

stops.name: The Vieux-Marché, the stake
stops.campa: In the morning Ladvenu brings the Body of Christ to her cell, and she cries to Cauchon: bishop, I die through you. On a plastered scaffold in the Old Market, mitred with the paper cap of heresy, she asks for a cross; an English soldier binds one of two sticks and she puts it in her breast, and Isambart holds the crucifix of Saint-Sauveur before her eyes in the smoke. She calls on her saints, forgives, and cries Jesus until the last. Her heart will not burn. The executioner tells the friars he has burned a saint; the ashes go into the Seine, which carries them to the sea.
stops.quote: Ah, Rouen, I greatly fear you may have to suffer for my death!... Jesus! Jesus!
stops.quote_source: Rehabilitation testimony of Jean Massieu, Isambart de la Pierre and Martin Ladvenu (1456)
